<reflection>
The first experiment provided kinetic data that fits many mechanisms almost equally well, with negative log-likelihood (NLL) values clustered around -20.15 to -20.04 for most candidates. Only M9, M11, and M20 show noticeably higher (less negative) NLL, indicating poorer fits, but the differences are still relatively small. This suggests that the initial condition (high substrate-to-catalyst ratio, no product) is not sufficient to discriminate among the diverse mechanistic hypotheses. My aim for this turn is to propose a second experiment that will perturb the system in a way that breaks degeneracies across multiple mechanisms simultaneously, rather than focusing on the top few.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among mechanisms that involve catalyst activation (M6, M8), dimerization (M2, M3, M5, M19), and various deactivation pathways (M9–M20), I propose an experiment with a tenfold lower catalyst concentration (0.001 M) and a small initial product concentration (0.1 M), while keeping substrate at 2.0 M. Lowering catalyst reduces the importance of bimolecular steps (e.g., dimerization, bimolecular deactivation), which should cause deviations from linear scaling of rate with catalyst if such steps are present. Adding product tests for reversibility and product inhibition, which are featured in many mechanisms (e.g., reversible M1, product inhibition M12, M17). This condition avoids extreme saturation or depletion, and it probes multiple mechanistic aspects at once—catalyst concentration dependence, reversibility, and inhibition—making it informative across a broad set of candidates.
</hypothesis>
